title: The hunter's night
hookLine: a hungry hunter waits all night in a tree, and the leaves he drops land somewhere he can't see
carry: shiva accepts even a vigil kept without knowing

cards: A hunter has caught nothing all day, and his family is waiting for food. Night comes. He climbs a tree beside a pool, where animals will come to drink, and settles in with his bow.
He's cold. He's hungry. He can't let himself sleep.
So his hands stay busy: he plucks leaves from the branches and lets them fall, one after another, into the dark below. He has no idea what's down there.
The story is told in the Shiva Purana, and retold on one particular night of the year.

teach.h: A BILVA TREE, A HIDDEN LINGA.
teach.b: Here is the turn, in paraphrase. The tree is a bilva tree, whose leaves are offered to Shiva. And at its foot, unseen in the dark, stands a Shiva linga.

All night long, the hunter's restless leaves fall onto it, along with drops of water. He stays awake through every watch of the night. It is Shivaratri, the great night of Shiva, though he doesn't know it.
When deer come to the water, he draws his bow, and each time he ends up letting them go. By morning, the story says, his heart has changed, and Shiva appears to him. He fasted because he had no food.
He kept vigil because he was afraid to sleep. He worshipped because his hands were fidgeting. The story is gentle about it.

teach.h: WHY SHIVARATRI IS KEPT THIS WAY.
teach.b: And that's why Maha Shivaratri is kept the way it is.
Hindus do on purpose what the hunter did by accident: they fast, stay awake through the watches of the night, pour water on the linga, offer bilva leaves, and often tell his story.
It's also why Shiva has a loving nickname, Bholenath, the simple, easily pleased lord. The rites matter, and people keep them with care.
But the story teaches that Shiva's grace runs ahead of our understanding: a night turned toward him counts, even half-understood. That's the second range in year four.

After the goddess comes Shiva: the Shiva Purana in selections, Nataraja the dancer, the Rudram, a first look at Kashmir Shaivism, and Maha Shivaratri itself, taught watch by watch, the way the hunter kept it without meaning to.

how: On Maha Shivaratri, devotees fast, keep vigil through the night, chant to Shiva, and offer water, milk and bilva leaves on the Shiva linga, and the story of the hunter is often retold.

games.q: on Maha Shivaratri your family stays up all night and offers bilva leaves on the linga. a friend asks where that comes from. what do you say?
o: it marks the night Durga defeated the buffalo demon.
it's from the hunter's story: he did all that by accident, and Shiva accepted it.
it's a harvest custom with no story behind it.
games.why: the hunter fasted, kept vigil and dropped bilva leaves on a hidden linga without knowing, and Shiva accepted the night. on Shivaratri, devotees do it on purpose.

practice: Rest your hands open on your knees, as if this were a short watch of the night.

Each time you breathe out, picture one leaf leaving your hand and falling into the dark, onto something you can't see, without needing to know where it lands. If you're tired, that's fine; the hunter was too.

wordCard.voice: Bilva. The tree whose leaves fell, by accident, on a hidden Shiva linga all through the night, the night a hunter kept without knowing it was holy.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: bilva, the tree whose leaves are offered to Shiva.

carryVoice: Your line: Shiva accepts even a vigil kept without knowing. The hunter never saw where his leaves fell. See you tomorrow.
